display_name: Paul Hobbs Richard Dinner Cuvee Agustina Chardonnay, Sonoma Mountain
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Perched above the fog line on the eastern slopes of Sonoma Mountain, the Richard Dinner Vineyard produces a Chardonnay defined by its struggle against Goulding clay loam and volcanic rock. This specific cuvée represents a selection of the vineyard’s most concentrated fruit, emphasizing structure over simple ripeness.",
  "wine_summary": "Paul Hobbs is a technician of site-specific winemaking, and the Richard Dinner Cuvee Agustina is his study of high-elevation intensity. Located within the Sonoma Mountain AVA, this vineyard sits at an elevation that keeps it bathed in sunlight while the valley floor below remains trapped in marine fog. This extended solar exposure allows for full phenolic ripeness—the development of complex flavor compounds—while the cooling winds from the Petaluma Gap preserve the acidity necessary to balance the wine's natural weight.\n\nThe wine is a departure from the broader, more tropical profiles found in warmer parts of the county. Because the vines are forced to root deeply into rocky, well-drained volcanic soils, the yields are naturally low. This creates a Chardonnay with a dense mid-palate and a distinct tactile grip that mirrors the rugged terrain of the mountain.",
  "terroir_expression": "The defining characteristic of this site is the volcanic soil mixed with rocky loam, which imparts a savory, almost saline edge to the fruit. Because the vineyard sits above 400 feet, the vines escape the dampness of the morning fog, leading to thicker grape skins and more concentrated juice. This elevation creates a significant diurnal shift—the difference between day and night temperatures—which ensures the wine retains a sharp malic acid backbone despite the richness gained from the afternoon sun.",
  "vinification_summary": "Hobbs employs native yeast fermentation and keeps the wine on its primary lees for 15 months, a process called sur lie aging that builds a creamy, toasted brioche texture. The wine undergoes full malolactic fermentation, where sharp malic acid is converted into softer lactic acid, yet the inherent mountain acidity prevents the profile from becoming flabby. Aging in approximately 50-60% new French oak provides a framework of baking spice and hazelnut without obscuring the citrus-driven core of the fruit.",
  "food_pairing": "Pair this with Miso-glazed Black Cod; the wine's weight matches the oily fish while the acidity cuts through the sugar in the glaze. For a casual option, Nashville Hot Chicken works because the residual richness and oak spice buffer the cayenne heat. In a fine dining setting, butter-poached lobster with a saffron emulsion highlights the wine's creamy texture and citrus top notes. Roasted chanterelle mushrooms on sourdough toast also complement the savory, volcanic undertones of the vineyard.",
  "comparable_wines": "Kistler Vineyards McCrea Vineyard Chardonnay — another high-elevation Sonoma Mountain site with similar volcanic tension. Peter Michael 'Belle Côte' Chardonnay — shares the same emphasis on power, density, and French oak integration. Mount Eden Vineyards Estate Chardonnay — offers a similar mountain-grown structure and longevity.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry white with high acidity and a dense, volcanic mineral core.",
  "cellar_recommendation": "While approachable after two years, this wine hits its peak between five and eight years. Store it at a consistent 55°F to allow the oak and fruit to integrate fully.",
  "value_assessment": "At $100 to $150 per bottle, this sits in the top tier of California Chardonnay alongside Aubert and Marcassin. It justifies the price by offering a level of concentration and site specificity that lower-priced bottlings from the Sonoma Coast lack. If you value structural power over easy-drinking fruit, the investment is sound.",
  "market_position": "This is a cornerstone for serious California collectors and appears on high-end steakhouse lists where it can compete with Grand Cru Burgundy. It appeals to the buyer who wants the weight of a traditional California Chardonnay but demands the precision of mountain viticulture.",
  "insider_take": "Skip this if you are looking for a lean, Chablis-style wine; this is unabashedly powerful and demands your attention. The real draw here isn't the butter—it's the dry extract and the way the volcanic soil makes the finish feel almost crunchy. It is a technical achievement that proves Sonoma Mountain can produce fruit as intense as any site in the Mayacamas.",
  "aging_potential_years": 12,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 3,

parsed.hook: Perched above the fog line on the eastern slopes of Sonoma Mountain, the Richard Dinner Vineyard produces a Chardonnay defined by its struggle against Goulding clay loam and volcanic rock. This specific cuvée represents a selection of the vineyard’s most concentrated fruit, emphasizing structure over simple ripeness.
parsed.wine_summary:
Paul Hobbs is a technician of site-specific winemaking, and the Richard Dinner Cuvee Agustina is his study of high-elevation intensity. Located within the Sonoma Mountain AVA, this vineyard sits at an elevation that keeps it bathed in sunlight while the valley floor below remains trapped in marine fog. This extended solar exposure allows for full phenolic ripeness—the development of complex flavor compounds—while the cooling winds from the Petaluma Gap preserve the acidity necessary to balance the wine's natural weight.

The wine is a departure from the broader, more tropical profiles found in warmer parts of the county. Because the vines are forced to root deeply into rocky, well-drained volcanic soils, the yields are naturally low. This creates a Chardonnay with a dense mid-palate and a distinct tactile grip that mirrors the rugged terrain of the mountain.
parsed.terroir_expression: The defining characteristic of this site is the volcanic soil mixed with rocky loam, which imparts a savory, almost saline edge to the fruit. Because the vineyard sits above 400 feet, the vines escape the dampness of the morning fog, leading to thicker grape skins and more concentrated juice. This elevation creates a significant diurnal shift—the difference between day and night temperatures—which ensures the wine retains a sharp malic acid backbone despite the richness gained from the afternoon sun.
parsed.vinification_summary: Hobbs employs native yeast fermentation and keeps the wine on its primary lees for 15 months, a process called sur lie aging that builds a creamy, toasted brioche texture. The wine undergoes full malolactic fermentation, where sharp malic acid is converted into softer lactic acid, yet the inherent mountain acidity prevents the profile from becoming flabby. Aging in approximately 50-60% new French oak provides a framework of baking spice and hazelnut without obscuring the citrus-driven core of the fruit.
parsed.food_pairing: Pair this with Miso-glazed Black Cod; the wine's weight matches the oily fish while the acidity cuts through the sugar in the glaze. For a casual option, Nashville Hot Chicken works because the residual richness and oak spice buffer the cayenne heat. In a fine dining setting, butter-poached lobster with a saffron emulsion highlights the wine's creamy texture and citrus top notes. Roasted chanterelle mushrooms on sourdough toast also complement the savory, volcanic undertones of the vineyard.
parsed.comparable_wines: Kistler Vineyards McCrea Vineyard Chardonnay — another high-elevation Sonoma Mountain site with similar volcanic tension. Peter Michael 'Belle Côte' Chardonnay — shares the same emphasis on power, density, and French oak integration. Mount Eden Vineyards Estate Chardonnay — offers a similar mountain-grown structure and longevity.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry white with high acidity and a dense, volcanic mineral core.
parsed.cellar_recommendation: While approachable after two years, this wine hits its peak between five and eight years. Store it at a consistent 55°F to allow the oak and fruit to integrate fully.
parsed.value_assessment: At $100 to $150 per bottle, this sits in the top tier of California Chardonnay alongside Aubert and Marcassin. It justifies the price by offering a level of concentration and site specificity that lower-priced bottlings from the Sonoma Coast lack. If you value structural power over easy-drinking fruit, the investment is sound.
parsed.market_position: This is a cornerstone for serious California collectors and appears on high-end steakhouse lists where it can compete with Grand Cru Burgundy. It appeals to the buyer who wants the weight of a traditional California Chardonnay but demands the precision of mountain viticulture.
parsed.insider_take: Skip this if you are looking for a lean, Chablis-style wine; this is unabashedly powerful and demands your attention. The real draw here isn't the butter—it's the dry extract and the way the volcanic soil makes the finish feel almost crunchy. It is a technical achievement that proves Sonoma Mountain can produce fruit as intense as any site in the Mayacamas.
